title: N-D-V

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-N-H: the soft answer, the poor one who is heard, and Moses, very meek. Your line was answer humbly. Did a soft answer turn anything away? Today, a gift nobody can require. Day one thousand four hundred ten.

Here is a fundraiser that had to be shut down for raising too much. The people in the wilderness are building the mishkan, the sanctuary, and they keep bringing gold, silver, yarn, linen, wood, every morning, more. Finally the craftsmen go to Moses and say: "The people bring much more than enough." So Moses has it announced through the whole camp: stop. And the text ends the scene with a line that's almost funny: "So the people were restrained from bringing." Restrained. From giving. Today's root is the kind of gift they couldn't stop bringing.

segments.voice: N-D-V. Nun, dalet, vet. Nedavah: a freewill gift, a voluntary offering. The verb: to give of your own accord, to volunteer. Turn it three ways. First, the instruction. When God asks for gifts for the sanctuary, the request is left open. Exodus says: "of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart ye shall take my offering." The gift is measured by the heart that moves it, not by the size. And when they bring it, the text calls it a willing offering, a nedavah, from men and women whose hearts made them willing. Second, the person. From the same letters comes nadiv: a generous person, and also a noble one. Isaiah says: "the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand." In that old English, liberal means generous, and the Hebrew is nadiv. Notice the verb: deviseth. The generous person plans generosity, thinks it up, the way someone else plans a business. Third, the difference. Jewish law also has giving that is required. Tzedakah, the giving to the poor, is commanded; the Torah's tithes are counted. A nedavah is the other thing: the gift nobody can require. Both matter in the tradition, and neither replaces the other. But the nedavah has its own shine. It's what happened in the wilderness when the people heard the request and simply kept coming, until someone had to ask them to stop. A free gift isn't free because it costs nothing. It's free because nobody made you.
screen: `WILLINGLY WITH HIS HEART.` · `NADIV: THE GENEROUS ONE PLANS IT.` · `OBLIGATION, AND THE GIFT BEYOND IT.` · `MORE THAN ENOUGH.` · then, large: `NOBODY MADE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give freely. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you could give today that nobody has asked you for and nobody expects. It doesn't have to be money. Time. A skill. A meal. A compliment you've been holding back. A note to a teacher from years ago. Let a few ideas come. Then pick one, and notice how it feels to choose it with no one requiring it. Plan it the way Isaiah's generous person devises: when, where, how. If you pray, you can offer it in your prayer. The bell holds the time.

segments.voice: N-D-V. Nun, dalet, vet: the root of nedavah, the freewill gift, and nadiv, the generous one. Today's word.
Your line: free gift. Today, give the one thing you planned, with no announcement and no expectation of anything back. Day one thousand four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Alongside obligatory tzedakah, Jewish tradition honors the nedavah, a gift given of one's own accord; the wilderness sanctuary in Exodus was built from such freewill offerings.
